extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic plays: how to construct plot, incident, recognition, and character to produce the effects of pity and fear. Covers structural parts of tragedy and artistic priorities (plot over spectacle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of the Situation (Peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject always to our rule of probability or necessity (e.g., messenger meant to cheer Oedipus but produces opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal must be probable or necessary within the plot. Best when combined with Recognition; produces powerful tragic effect (pity/fear). Examples: Oedipus, Lynceus. Do not make reversals gratuitous or irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune; best when coincident with a Reversal of the Situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition most effective when intimately connected with the plot (especially recognition of persons). It should arise from the action and produce pity or fear. Various forms exist (tokens, incident, memory, reasoning); some are more artistic than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: A destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily agony, wounds, and the like) that is an element of the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such incidents when they arise naturally from the plot. They are one component of producing tragedy but must be integrated plausibly and not merely spectacularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative Parts of Tragedy (Prologos, Episode, Exodos, Parodos, Stasimon, Commos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into parts: Prologos (entire part preceding the Parodos), Episode (part between choric songs), Exodos (part with no choric song after it); Parodos (first utterance of Chorus), Stasimon (choric ode without certain meters), Commos (joint lament of Chorus and actors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the standard divisions the poet should employ and recognize when constructing the play. Some songs (actors' stage-songs, Commos) are peculiar to some plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex rather than Simple Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should be arranged not on the simple but on the complex plan; the complex plot includes Reversal and Recognition and produces pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots (with complication and unravelling connected) are superior. Simple plots lack the emotional power proper to tragedy. The complication and its resolution should arise from the plot itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Subject-Matter: middle character and error (hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune should not be the spectacle of a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity, nor of a bad man passing from adversity to prosperity, nor the downfall of an utter villain; rather it should be a man 'between' these extremes whose misfortune is brought about not by vice but by some error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a protagonist like Oedipus — illustrious and prosperous but fallible. Such a figure arouses pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (a man like ourselves). Avoid extremes that fail to provoke pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singleness of Issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single in its issue (single outcome) rather than double; the change of fortune should be from good to bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a unified, single-threaded outcome. Double-thread or opposite catastrophes (good and bad endings in same play) may flatter weak audiences but do not produce the true tragic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of Inner Structure over Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity may be aroused by spectacular means, but they may also result from the inner structure of the piece, which is the better way; the poet should aim that the tale told (without sight) still thrills with horror and melts to pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on spectacle to create the tragic effect; integrate the tragic quality into incidents and plot. Spectacular methods can create the monstrous rather than the tragic and are less artistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances That Produce Pity and Fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing pity and fear must happen between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent; the strongest effects arise when the incident occurs between persons who are near or dear to one another (kinship, e.g., brother killing brother, son killing father, mother her son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek incidents involving intimate ties to maximize pity/fear. If an enemy kills an enemy or indifferent persons act, less pity is evoked except for the suffering itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic handling of traditional material
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may not destroy the framework of received legends (e.g., that Clytemnestra was slain by Orestes) but ought to show invention of his own and skilfully handle traditional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established stories/families (a few houses) because they contain moving incidents, but exercise invention and skill in presentation and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why certain ways of committing the deed are better or worse
rubrics_metrics.description: The deed (horrible action) may be: (1) done consciously with knowledge of the persons; (2) done in ignorance with discovery afterward; (3) about to be done with knowledge and then not done (worst—shocking but not tragic); (4) about to be done in ignorance and discovered before action (best in some cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rank these artistically: best is perpetrated in ignorance with discovery afterward (startling effect without prior shock); worst is aborted action with knowledge (shocking but not tragic). Choose the mode that best serves pity/fear and the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character aims (four points): goodness, propriety, likeness to life, consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of character there are four things to be aimed at: (1) goodness (character's purpose expresses moral goodness relative to class), (2) propriety (suitable traits for sex/class/role), (3) truth to life (characters should be believable), (4) consistency (even if the subject is inconsistent, the portrayal must be consistently inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure speech/actions manifest moral purpose; maintain appropriate masculine/feminine roles and social types; avoid motiveless degradation, indecorous traits, or erratic changes (examples cited: Menelaus, Iphigenia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions must follow by necessity or probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the complication and the unravelling, and the conduct of characters, should arise out of the plot itself by necessary or probable sequence rather than by chance or irrationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrational events within the action; if irrational elements exist, keep them outside the drama's scope. The plot's causal logic must feel necessary or at least probable to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deus ex Machina limited use
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deus ex Machina (divine machine) must not be used to resolve the drama's internal issues; it should be employed only for events external to the drama—antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use external contrivances to unravel the plot; resolution should come from within the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition: ranked types and artistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Kinds of recognition (least to most artistic): (1) recognition by signs/tokens (congenital or acquired marks, scars, necklaces); (2) recognition by a turn of incident (more artistic, e.g., Bath Scene); (3) recognitions invented by the poet (speaking revelations — near allied to tokens and less artistic); (4) by memory (emotion awakened by sight/sound); (5) by process of reasoning (inference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that arise from incident or natural memory/reasoning over formal tokens or poet-contrived speeches. Strive for recognitions that feel necessary to the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic pleasure defined as pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctive mark of tragic imitation is that it imitates actions which excite pity and fear; the poet's purpose is to produce this pleasure through imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the play by whether it successfully elicits pity and fear; other pleasures (e.g., spectacle, monstrous shock) are not the proper aim of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of sensory appeals is secondary but important
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses (spectacle, song, etc.) are not among essentials but are concomitants of poetry and leave room for error; they should not substitute for essential plot/character virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory elements to support, not replace, the inner structure; mistakes here can mar otherwise well-constructed tragedies.
